name: CULTIGEN
fullname: CULture, TourIsm, reGENeration through innovative digital solutions and governance platforms
description: The CULTIGEN project aims to develop sustainable strategies to manage tourism flows, prevent overtourism, and align residents' needs with visitors' expectations. Part of this is creating incentives for tourists to leave the inner city of Copenhagen and visit selected micro-destinations outside the city center. Our role in the project is to develop and ’Urban Listening Toolkit’ that uses mobile etnography and digital methods to get a sense of locals perceptions of the values in the chosen micro-destinations as well as the types of tourism offers that would align well with the atmosphere in the area. Or make visible contrasting vies of what that atmosphere is. This includes working with data from Google Maps, AirBnB and qualitative narratives from the Urban Belonging App. By involving both Copenhagen residents and tourists, the project seeks to build a collaborative, inclusive, and sustainable model for tourism management. CULTIGEN is an Innovative Actions project under the European Urban Initiative, running from December 2024 to May 2028 with a total budget of 35 million kroner. CULTIGEN is led by The City of Copenhagen. In the consortium we collaborate with Aalborg University, the National Museum of Denmark, StoryHunt, We Do Democrazy, and Wonderful Copenhagen.

name: Datalands
fullname: Hyperscale datacentres and the transformation of place
description: To include hard-to-measure aspects of place and community life into planning decisions regarding datacenters to avoid polarisation.

name: AWARE
fullname: AI in the Welfare state: Accountability and Responsibility at stake
description: to generate knowledge that can help Danish municipalities respond to the risk of artificial intelligence (AI) eroding accountability relations among caseworkers and citizens.

name: MOVEO
fullname: Intelligent Framework for Inclusive and Seamless Transport Infrastructure and Mobility Services
description: The Horizon Europe funded MOVEO project proposes a scalable intelligent framework designed to foster inclusive, efficient, and seamless transport infrastructure and mobility services, bringing together engineers, planners, managers, and researchers across 16 institutions and 9 countries. One of the project’s priorities is accessibility and inclusiveness, extending both to the physical design of transport systems and to the digital services that inform and support users. This is where our research group contributes. We investigate how studying perspectives of accessibility can inform inclusive planning in the context of sustainable transportation. Our research is driven by a methodological ambition to find new ways of giving voice to perspectives that are divergent and often excluded, simplified, or muted in bureaucratic processes. By tuning GenAI and RAG algorithms on multimedia documentation of images, texts, voice notes, and metadata of time and space, we introduce what we call "perspectival models" (Underwood, 2019). Drawing on recent explorations of bringing perspectives into interaction using AI (Kozlowski & Evans, 2025; Nelson, 2021; Noyman et al., 2025), we reflect upon in what ways they could succeed in involving citizens’ voices in urban planning. Are they able to convey citizens’ ideas? Or do they merely serve as an elicitation device?
tags: digital methods;computational humanities;urban planning;public transportation;public participation;perspectival modelling

name: STÅSTEDER
fullname: Perspectival Models for Cultural Sustainability in Democratic Green Transition Processes
description: STÅSTEDER develops new AI-based methods for bringing citizens' diverse perspectives earlier and more systematically into democratic decision-making processes concerning the green transition. The project is motivated by the observation that existing decision-support models are primarily based on economic incentives and assumptions of rational behaviour, while the cultural values and lived worlds that shape citizens’ understandings of environmental problems are often overlooked. The project develops what we call perspectival models. These are respondent-validated AI agents trained to emulate particular ways of seeing and interpreting the world. A perspective is here understood as an analytical distillation of a specific standpoint, while recognising that individuals embody multiple, and sometimes contradictory, standpoints at the same time. The aim is to investigate the democratic potential of such models. First, they may foster timely openness by helping public administrations identify relevant perspectives before problem definitions and proposed solutions become fixed. Second, they can function as virtual proxies, giving voice to citizens and viewpoints that are not present in the room. Third, they can provide continuous depth by preserving insight into the experiences, values and rationalities that underpin people's opinions throughout the planning and policy process. From a research perspective, STÅSTEDER examines both how such models can be made accountable to the people whose perspectives they represent and how they might generate productive dissonance by challenging established assumptions and broadening understandings of complex sustainability challenges. At the same time, the project critically investigates the challenges and risks involved in integrating AI into public administration in this way, including questions of legitimacy, representation, trust and democratic accountability.

name: LOGICARE
description: LOGICARE studies the taken-for-granted yet vital logistics that make healthcare possible: how the right supplies arrive in the right place at the right time. This has become especially important as hospitals try to reduce costs while treating more patients more quickly. I argue that this challenge is not simply a technical matter with one rational solution. It is also a question of values: how different actors define what counts as “good” logistics. A hospital manager concerned with costs, for example, may have different priorities than a nurse who needs to be prepared for unforeseen complications. My project studies logistics and clinical staff, and how they negotiate logistical priorities in everyday hospital operations. By doing so, we will better understand how value judgments made in the background shape the efficiency, sustainability and quality of care at the frontline.

name: EASY-GEN
fullname: Easy Workflow Integration for Gene Therapy
description: CAR-T cell therapy is highly complex, time-consuming, and costly, partly because cells are currently manufactured through centralised and logistically demanding processes. EASYGEN aims to develop a faster, automated platform for producing CAR-T cells directly in hospitals, reducing the time from cell collection to treatment. The STS component of the project examines how this technological transition reshapes hospital work, care pathways, and logistical arrangements. Through co-creation with clinicians and other healthcare workers, we will explore how the new system can be meaningfully integrated into everyday practice. The aim is to develop a human-centred approach to CAR-T logistics, one that addresses not only efficiency and scalability, but also the experiences, needs, and working conditions of patients and professionals.

name: ECHO Games
description: The ECHO Games Working Group explores games as tools for research, public engagement, and participation. Drawing on STS and game-design perspectives, the group examines how games are worlding science, technology, and society. At the same time, the group tests games as tools to explore those worlds. Games can enable players to inhabit situated perspectives, navigate conflicting goals, and explore alternative possibilities. The group meets regularly to play, discuss, and test existing games and experimental prototypes, share relevant literature and projects, and explore what games can contribute to understanding and shaping the worlds we inhabit. Members also develop their own games to communicate research questions, engage publics and stakeholders, and generate new insights in the research process.

name: Good-by-Devicing
fullname: Probing how value comes to matter in the energy transition
description: While the climate crisis accentuates the need to decouple economies from fossil fuels, local opposition in Europe increasingly delays the transition to renewable energy. Arguing that the energy transition has been organised as an expert issue pursued by design tools based in techno-economic valuation, Good-by-Devicing proposes that resistance to renewable energy cannot be solved when opposition has already solidified in the phase of project planning and development. Instead, this project seeks to accommodate broader social concerns over the impacts of the energy transition much earlier, by inquiring into the design phase where experts develop and use critical design tools such as energy scenarios, digital simulations, and procurement schemes. These devices incorporate expert decisions on what concerns to include and exclude in the design of the energy transition. Hypothesising that rising opposition has roots in colliding valuations of the value of energy transition and what concerns should be accounted for, Good-by-Devicing probes a position where renewable energy can be deployed with sufficient pace, but where broader social values are encompassed in the design tools that shape our energy future. To shed light on how value comes to matter in the energy transition, the project uses the case of the world’s largest energy islands planned for operation by 2030 in Denmark, using the inhabited natural island of Bornholm as a strategic research site to ask how the energy transition could be valued otherwise, encompassing broader social concerns. Combining perspectives in Science & Technology Studies of Valuation Studies and the Sociology of Expertise, the project provides a new understanding of local opposition to renewables, contributing to the Social Acceptance literature, as well as to Valuation Studies and its new notion of the good economy, exploring how the ‘good fossil-free society’ could be "re-deviced" to account for social concerns, thereby reducing conflict.

name: Expertise of Expectations
description: The objective of the Expertise of Expectations (EoE) project is to increase our understanding of how different forms of expertise mould expectations of the future. Decisions on which types of concerns and valuations to consider in the shaping and making of expected future(s) are explored through the case of Power-to-X (PtX) technologies that rely on expertises coming together. Scientific and public controversy are often prevalent when expected futures are being formed and contested. Controversies are therefore places where dynamics of expertise(s) can be observed to shift over time and investigated in how they are maintained and enacted by different kinds of expertise. A new theoretical lens is forged of three strands of STS research - i.e., Valuation Studies, Networks of Expertise, and the Sociology of Expectations - that lets us investigate expertise, technology and market together. This new combination provides analytical tools to examine how expertise (e)valuatively charges expectations and renders expectations with agency. Not only is it relevant for valuation struggles of current design of the good energy future, but also to inform how we might go differently about coming together when forming expected future(s).

name: CXAI
description: The problem of explaining outputs of black-boxed AI systems has become central to the discussion around how to ensure alignment with human interests and values. It has become standard practice to explain the behavioral patterns of these models as the result of cultural biases in their training data, and to frame alignment as a matter of creating models that resemble or "share" the values of their users. Yet a significant knowledge gap exists regarding the theoretical and empirical basis for both kinds of explanation. CXAI is a research project funded by the Independent Research Fund Denmark (DFF), which aims to develop theories and methods for studying AI-human relations from an anthropological perspective, where the notion of "explainability" is itself taken to be part of the research object. The theories, ontologies and sense-making practices that undergird prominent ideas about how to understand and develop culturally aligned AI models are understood as part of the nexus that makes up AI culture. Conversely, the way cultural data (texts, images) is internalized through the training pipelines of large language models, and eventually partakes in the cultural encounter with humans, is taken to be part of that same nexus.

name: Observatory
fullname: The Observatory for Technological Questions in Society
description: The observatory maps technological debates in Debnmark and provides ongoing anlayses. It is a collaboration between ECHOlab and the central communications office at DTU. We monitor technological controversies on a weekly basis and use it to stengthen DTU's presence and engagement in such debates. The aim is to test a range of communication formats that will explore how DTU can help qualify the democratic conversation on technology, begins from the questions and concerns that actors in society raise, and to develop an LLM-supported pipeline in support of this.

name: IPCC
fullname: Mapping the Epistemic Geographies of the IPCC
description: This projects investigates what kinds of expertise - and in particular how shifting communities of experts - influence the work of the International Panel on Climate Change. Our work package is particularly focussed on scientometric analysis of both the scientific litterature and lines of sight (citation patterns) directly in the IPCC reports.

name: Valuing Sustainability
description: A double special issue on "Valuing Sustainability" (Heimstädt and Schneider, forthcoming) in Valuation Studies examining how sustainability is valued across a wide range of cases including sheep farming, ecotoxicology, basic research, microplastics, nuclear waste, wind energy, housing, AI, agricultural technology, microbial cleaning products, corporate sustainability, and pension funds. Across these diverse cases, the special issue shows that while calls to promote sustainability are widespread, they often fail to address the root causes of the socio-ecological crisis. Instead of interpreting this merely as greenwashing, the special issue approaches it as a valuation problem and outlines an agenda for a valuation studies of sustainability.

name: DigiFront
fullname: Transnational Collaboration at the Digital Frontier
description: Transnational Collaboration at the Digital Frontier (in short: Digi Front) is a research project that starts from the premise that public sector digitalization is increasingly driven by transnational collaboration and asks how best practices of digital government travel across national contexts, and what kind of politically and culturally transformative effects this may have on national welfare states? The circulating best practices of digital government have an unacknowledged political character, as the process of public digitalization does not just streamline the welfare state but also fundamentally transforms the internal working of the state as well as the relations to its citizens, the private sector and other countries. An STS-informed study, the project theorises public digitalization as a transnational network of artefacts, expertise, and events and ethnographically follows three countries deeply engaged in knowledge sharing.

name: Chronic Pain AI
description: This is an alliance PhD project (2024-2027) between Cornell University and DTU. In a multi-sited ethnography, Amelie studies how automation reshapes chronic pain care. She is interested automated opioid risk assessment reconfigures notions of risk in U.S. opioid prescribing. She follows how chronic care trajectories turn citizens into chronic organisers of time in the Danish welfare state. Her current work delves into the epistemic and experimental setups of the pain lab, where she follows the development of automated pain sensing technologies. Across these sites, she attends to the epistemic work that is done to make pain amenable to automation, but also to practices of resistance against them. Pain is difficult to manage. This project seeks to show what happens when automation is posed as the answer, and its stakes.

name: Venture Capitalization
description: A themed section on "Venture Capitalization as Zeitgeist" (Riom and Schneider, forthcoming) in the Journal of Cultural Economy examining how speculative logics of valuation extend beyond venture capital investors and start-up firms to shape practices, relations, and expectations of socio-economic development and progress over time. This themed section argues that venture capital is not merely a mechanism for raising funds for start-ups or a passing trend but rather has longer-term structural and socio-cultural effects that extend the logics and interests of finance deep into non-financial domains. By conceptualising venture capitalisation as a zeitgeist, the themed section proposes a framework for diagnosing the political and economic crises that characterise contemporary capitalism.

name: Talk Walks
description: Monthly talk walks to stay au courant with the latest publiucations in digital methods and related fields (computational humanities, social studies of AI, social data science, etc.). We read 3 recent papers, walk for 2 hours, spend half an hour on each paper and have time for a snack. We split in smaller groups and discuss main takeaways and implications for our own research for 20 minutes, then share collectively for 10 minutes. New groups for each paper.

name: Research Seminars
description: The research seminar series is our common place for STS research. Every Friday from 13-14, we meet and take turns presenting our work in different formats, including paper draft sessions, data sessions, and presentations. Here, we learn about each other's work, discuss it, and provide valuable feedback. We also regularly invite STS scholars from other institutions.
